title: Why do Godement--Jacquet and Rankin--Selberg conductors match?
question:
Let $F$ be a non-archimedean local field, let $\Pi$ be a generic representation of $GL_n(F)$ in its Whittaker model, and let $\pi$ be a generic representation of $GL_m(F)$. The Godement--Jacquet integral yields a conductor exponent $c_{\mathrm{GJ}}(\Pi \times \pi)=c(\Pi)+c(\pi)$, while the Rankin--Selberg integral on Whittaker functions defines its own exponent through the epsilon factor $\varepsilon(s,\Pi \times \pi,\psi)=\omega(\Pi \times \pi,\psi)\,q^{-c_{\mathrm{RS}}(\Pi \times \pi)(s-\tfrac12)}$. Take $W_0$ to be the Casselman new vector of $\Pi$ normalized so that $W_0(gk)=W_0(g)$ for every $k \in K_1(\mathfrak{p}^{c(\Pi)})$.

Why must $c_{\mathrm{RS}}(\Pi \times \pi)$ coincide with $c_{\mathrm{GJ}}(\Pi \times \pi)$ once we pair $W_0$ with the new vector of $\pi$ and translate by any allowed unipotent element $u_Q$, and how do the epsilon factor constraints certify that $R(u_Q)W_0$ remains nonzero across the required support cells?
answer:
On the Godement--Jacquet side, choosing new vectors $v_0$ for $\Pi$ and $w_0$ for $\pi$ means the matrix coefficient used in the zeta integral is fixed by $K_1(\mathfrak{p}^{c(\Pi)}) \times K_1(\mathfrak{p}^{c(\pi)})$. The Bruhat-Schwartz test function can therefore be taken to be the characteristic function of the corresponding compact cosets, so the local functional equation forces the conductor to be $c_{\mathrm{GJ}}(\Pi \times \pi)=c(\Pi)+c(\pi)$.

Passing to the Rankin--Selberg model, Casselman--Shalika describes $W_0$ explicitly on $N(F)T^{+}K_1(\mathfrak{p}^{c(\Pi)})$. Translating by $u_Q$ shifts only the $N$-component, so $R(u_Q)W_0(g)=W_0(gu_Q)$ never vanishes on the dominant torus, and the resulting Whittaker section is still fixed by $K_1(\mathfrak{p}^{c(\Pi)})$. When we pair it with the new vector $W_{\pi}$ supported on $K_1(\mathfrak{p}^{c(\pi)})$, the nonzero torus cells in $N(F)T^{+}$ pick up valuation factors exactly equal to $q^{-c(\Pi)(s-1/2)}q^{-c(\pi)(s-1/2)}$, showing $c_{\mathrm{RS}}(\Pi \times \pi)=c(\Pi)+c(\pi)$.

Finally, the epsilon factor normalization $\varepsilon(s,\Pi \times \pi,\psi)=\omega(\Pi \times \pi,\psi)\,q^{-c_{\mathrm{RS}}(\Pi \times \pi)(s-1/2)}$ couples the Rankin--Selberg integral with the Godement--Jacquet functional equation. If $R(u_Q)W_0$ vanished on any required cell, the Rankin--Selberg epsilon factor would drop in valuation and contradict the Godement--Jacquet value. Because the functional equation is unique, the equality of epsilon factors certifies that $c_{\mathrm{RS}}=c_{\mathrm{GJ}}$ and that every permitted $u_Q$ keeps $R(u_Q)W_0$ nonzero on the support needed to realize the matched conductor.

nodes.text: if R(u_Q) acts on W_0 then the support stays nonzero
